explanation: The crus cerebri (basis pedunculi) forms the anterolateral boundary of the interpeduncular fossa. It contains the corticospinal, corticobulbar, and corticopontine fibers.
keyConcept: Crus cerebri forms anterolateral boundary of interpeduncular fossa

explanation: The abducent nerve (CN VI) has the most medial attachment to the pons, emerging in the median line at the pontomedullary junction. The facial and vestibulocochlear nerves attach more laterally.
keyConcept: Abducent nerve most medial pontine attachment

explanation: The vestibulocochlear nerve attaches at the cerebellopontine angle, which is the angle between the pons, cerebellum, and medulla. This is the correct matching for the anatomical location.
keyConcept: CN VIII at cerebellopontine angle

explanation: The hypoglossal nerve attaches in the sulcus between the olive and inferior cerebellar peduncle. This is a posterior attachment, not between pyramid and olive. The statement is incorrect about the groove location.
keyConcept: CN XII between olive and ICP

explanation: The vagus nerve (CN X) lies MEDIAL to the inferior cerebellar peduncle. Rootlets emerge between the olive and the inferior cerebellar peduncle. The statement in option D incorrectly places it lateral to ICP.
keyConcept: Vagus nerve medial to inferior cerebellar peduncle

explanation: Cerebellopontine angle tumors typically arise from the vestibulocochlear nerve (acoustic neuroma/schwannoma) and cause hearing loss, vertigo, and later facial nerve involvement. Pontine gliomas would cause different symptoms.
keyConcept: CPA tumors cause deafness and vertigo

explanation: The optic nerve is an outpouching of the brain and does not wind around the cerebral peduncles; it runs in the optic tract to the lateral geniculate body. The trochlear nerve wraps around the cerebral peduncle.
keyConcept: Optic nerve does not wind around cerebral peduncle

explanation: The optic nerve is not a boundary of the interpeduncular fossa. The boundaries are: cerebral peduncles (posterolateral), upper border of pons (inferior), optic chiasma (superior), and optic tract (posterolateral).
keyConcept: Optic nerve not boundary of interpeduncular fossa

explanation: The interpeduncular fossa is located in the midbrain, between the cerebral peduncles. Its contents (oculomotor nerve, posterior perforated substance, etc.) are all midbrain structures.
keyConcept: Interpeduncular fossa belongs to midbrain

explanation: The vestibular trigone lies between the limbs of the inferior fovea in the floor of the fourth ventricle. This is the correct statement about dorsal medullary surface features.
keyConcept: Vestibular trigone between limbs of inferior fovea

explanation: The medial eminence overlies the abducent nucleus, not the facial nucleus. The facial nucleus lies more laterally and is overlain by the facial colliculus formed by fibers wrapping around the abducent nucleus.
keyConcept: Medial eminence overlies abducent nucleus, not facial

explanation: This matching tests knowledge of fourth ventricle boundaries: Superior medullary velum forms the superior roof; facial colliculus is in the pontine floor; inferior cerebellar peduncle forms lateral boundary; choroid plexus forms inferior roof; inferior fovea is in the medial floor.
keyConcept: Superior medullary velum forms superior roof of 4th ventricle

explanation: Posterior external arcuate fibers originate from the accessory cuneate nucleus (lateral cuneate nucleus), which receives proprioceptive input from the upper limb. These fibers enter the cerebellum via the inferior cerebellar peduncle.
keyConcept: Accessory cuneate nucleus gives posterior arcuate fibers

explanation: A lemniscus is a collection of sensory fibers that ascend through the brainstem. Examples include the medial lemniscus (fine touch/proprioception), spinal lemniscus (pain/temperature), and trigeminal lemniscus (face sensation).
keyConcept: Lemniscus is collection of ascending fibers in brainstem

explanation: The descending tracts (corticospinal, corticobulbar) run in the crus cerebri of the midbrain. The tegmentum contains ascending tracts and nuclei. The substantia nigra separates the crus from the tegmentum.
keyConcept: Descending tracts in crus cerebri

explanation: Internal arcuate fibers are axons of second-order neurons in the dorsal column nuclei (gracile and cuneate nuclei). They decussate in the medulla to form the medial lemniscus.
keyConcept: Internal arcuate fibers from gracile/cuneate nuclei

explanation: The frontal pontine fibers (from prefrontal cortex) occupy the medial one-fifth of the crus cerebri. Corticospinal fibers are in the middle three-fifths, and parieto/temporopontine fibers are in the lateral one-fifth.
keyConcept: Frontopontine fibers in medial 1/5 of crus cerebri

explanation: The medial accessory olive is part of the olivary nuclear complex within the medulla. The superior olivary nucleus is in the pons, not the medulla.
keyConcept: Superior olivary nucleus not in medulla

explanation: The medial longitudinal fasciculus connects the vestibular nuclei with the nuclei of cranial nerves III, IV, and VI to coordinate eye movements. It also connects with the spinal cord for head and neck reflexes.
keyConcept: MLF connects vestibular nuclei with III, IV, VI nuclei

explanation: This matching tests midbrain structures: cerebral aqueduct (around which the tectal plate curves); trochlear nucleus (inferior to oculomotor); superior cerebellar peduncle (lateral to red nucleus).
keyConcept: Superior cerebellar peduncle decussates in midbrain

explanation: The nucleus ambiguus is the motor nucleus supplying muscles of the larynx (and pharynx/soft palate). It is the common motor nucleus for cranial nerves IX, X, and XI for these muscles.
keyConcept: Nucleus ambiguus supplies laryngeal muscles

explanation: The nucleus solitarius (solitary nucleus) is the visceral afferent nucleus receiving general visceral afferent (GVA) and special visceral afferent (SVA - taste) fibers from CN VII, IX, and X.
keyConcept: Nucleus solitarius - visceral afferent column

explanation: The nucleus ambiguus is the special visceral efferent (branchiomotor) nucleus for cranial nerves IX, X, and XI. It supplies stylopharyngeus (IX), pharynx/larynx muscles (X), and sternocleidomastoid/trapezius (XI).
keyConcept: Nucleus ambiguus - common motor for IX, X, XI

explanation: The nucleus solitarius receives taste fibers (special visceral afferent) from the facial, glossopharyngeal, and vagus nerves. It is the only nucleus dedicated to visceral afferent processing.
keyConcept: Nucleus solitarius receives taste fibers

explanation: The muscles NOT supplied by nucleus ambiguus include the tensor tympani and tensor veli palatini, which are branchiomotor muscles of the trigeminal nerve (motor V).
keyConcept: Nucleus ambiguus does not supply tensor muscles
